papers.title_in_file: Simulation-Based Approach to Efficient Commonsense Reasoning in Very Large Knowledge Bases
papers.what_it_is: A Cycorp paper that learns an inference-step ordering heuristic for the Cyc knowledge base with Monte Carlo tree search (UCT) plus k-nearest-neighbor generalization, and reports speedup and answered-query gains on 1022 real queries.

assertions.value: The authors describe a search heuristic that uses a Monte-Carlo simulation technique to choose inference steps, and test it on the Cyc knowledge base.
quotes: we describe a search heuristic that uses a Monte-Carlo simulation technique to choose inference steps
We test the efficacy of this approach on a very large and expressive commonsense KB, Cyc.
assertions.certainty_reason: The abstract and introduction state the paper's own method and test bed.

assertions.value: The authors state that the key idea is to simulate several thousand paths from a node, and that each node in the search tree holds a value that is the average number of answers from all simulated paths that visit that node.
quotes: The key idea is to simulate several thousand paths from a node.
These values are simply the average number of answers from all simulated paths that visit that node.
assertions.certainty_reason: The introduction defines the node value used by the method.

assertions.value: The authors claim that the evaluation function is not handcrafted and depends solely on the outcomes of simulated paths, and that the approach is a statistical anytime algorithm whose evaluation function improves with additional simulations.
quotes: the evaluation function is not handcrafted: It depends solely on the outcomes of the simulated paths.
The quality of evaluation function improves with additional simulations.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim; the paper reports no experiment that isolates this property directly.
assertions.reader_inference: The experiments vary the number of simulations (Figures 2 to 5), but the figures are images, so the text layer does not hold the curves that would support the anytime claim.

assertions.value: The authors state that, in contrast to premise-selection work, they focus on designing ordering heuristics that enable the system to work with all axioms.
quotes: In contrast, we focus on designing ordering heuristics that will enable the system to work with all axioms.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the scope of their own approach in Related Work.

assertions.value: The authors claim that their approach differs from all the earlier work they list because none of it has shown how a Monte Carlo tree search/UCT-based approach can be used to improve reasoning in a very large and expressive knowledge-based system.
quotes: Our approach is different from all aforementioned research because none have shown how Monte Carlo tree search/UCT-based approach can be used to improve reasoning in a very large and expressive KBS.
assertions.certainty_reason: A novelty claim by the authors with no evidence beyond the paper's own literature list.

assertions.value: The authors state that, because of the intractability of reasoning in very large expressive knowledge bases, even simple queries are timed out after several minutes, and they report that researchers believe resolution-based theorem provers are overwhelmed on large expressive knowledge bases.
quotes: Due to the intractability of reasoning in such systems, even simple queries are timed-out after several minutes.
are overwhelmed when they are expected to work on large expressive KBs
assertions.certainty_reason: A motivating statement by the authors, attributed in part to Hoder and Voronkov 2011, not tested in this paper.

assertions.value: The authors report that researchers have shown that the specific order of node and rule expansion can have a significant effect on efficiency, citing Tsarkov and Horrocks.
quotes: researchers have shown that the specific order of node and rule expansion can have a significant effect on efficiency
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Cyc knowledge base has 27.3 million assertions and 1.14 million individuals.
quotes: The KB has 27.3 million assertions and 1.14 million individuals.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors, from the company that builds Cyc, describe their own product.

assertions.value: The authors state that the number of rules in Cyc with three, four and five variables is 48160, 23813 and 14014 respectively, and that 29716 rules have more than five variables.
quotes: The number of rules in Cyc with three, four, and five variables is 48160, 23813 and 14014 respectively.
Moreover, 29716 rules have more than five variables.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors, from the company that builds Cyc, describe their own product.

assertions.value: The authors state that Cyc has more than 2000 rules with quantification over predicates and 267 relations with variable arities, and that first-order logic with three variables is undecidable (citing Tsarkov et al.) while Cyc has several thousand rules with more than three variables.
quotes: Cyc has more than 2000 rules with quantification over predicates, (b) It has 267 relations with variable arities
Cyc has several thousand rules with more than three variables
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors, from the company that builds Cyc, describe their own product; the undecidability statement is cited.

assertions.value: The authors define a heuristic module as a tuple of a weight and a function that assesses the quality of an inference step, and state that Cyc uses a set of heuristic modules to identify the best clause from the set of support.
quotes: Cyc uses a set of heuristic modules to identify the best clause from the set of support.

assertions.certainty_reason: The Background section defines the heuristic module used by the baseline and the new method.

assertions.value: The authors state that Cyc uses several heuristics including the success rate of rules, decision trees, regression-based models and a large database of useful rule sequences, and that in its default inference mode Cyc uses the policy function pi-BASELINE, which serves as the baseline in the experiments.
quotes: Cyc uses several heuristics including the success rate of rules, decision trees
In its default inference mode, Cyc uses a policy function, π BASELINE (s), to guide the search.
This is used as the “baseline” in the experiments discussed below.
assertions.certainty_reason: The Background section states the comparison baseline of the experiments.

assertions.value: The authors formulate proof search as a sequence of states and actions that continues without backtracking until a terminal state with an outcome is reached, and the aim of the reasoner is to maximize that outcome.
quotes: sampling of states and actions continues, without
backtracking, until the search finishes upon reaching a
The aim of the reasoner is to
assertions.certainty_reason: The Background section defines the search problem used by the method.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer splits these quotes across lines; the word maximize and the terminal-state outcome sit on adjacent lines.

assertions.value: The authors state that Q(s, a) denotes the value of selecting action a in state s and is simply the expected reward of that action, computed from simulation outcomes.
quotes: simply the expected reward of action
is used to denote the value of selecting action
assertions.certainty_reason: The Background section defines Q(s, a) used by the method.

assertions.value: The authors state that the search tree contains a node for each state generated during simulations, and each state in the tree stores three types of values, N(s), N(s, a) and Q(s, a) for every applicable action a.
quotes: The search tree contains a node for each state
Each state
stores three types of values: N(s), N(s, a) and Q(s, a) for every action
assertions.certainty_reason: The section defines the statistics the tree stores.

assertions.value: The authors describe the simulation algorithm as two phases: a tree policy is used until depth d, and a default policy completes the simulation beyond depth d; the outcome of the simulation is backed up through the selected nodes to update their statistics.
quotes: When the depth of a node is greater than d
the outcome of the simulation is “backed up” through the selected nodes to update their statistics.
assertions.certainty_reason: The section defines the algorithm that the experiments run.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper does not state the value of the depth cutoff d used in the experiments.

assertions.value: The authors state that the tree policy uses the UCT algorithm to build a tree over the state space with the current state as the root node, that an action never selected before is chosen first, and that otherwise UCT selects the action that maximizes an upper confidence bound with a Q(s, a) term and an exploration term scaled by the parameter c.
quotes: use the UCT algorithm to build a tree over the state space
selecting it before any sampled action. Otherwise, the UCT
The first term in (2), Q(s, a), favors actions that have led to better outcomes in the past.
assertions.certainty_reason: The Tree policy paragraph defines the selection rule used.

assertions.value: The authors state that the exploration parameter c helps bias the search toward or against exploration, and that they report experiments showing how performance changes with c.
quotes: helps us in biasing the search toward or against exploration
we report results of several experiments that show how performance changes with c.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paragraph defines the role of c in the experiments.

assertions.value: The authors state that Cyc's existing mechanism for selecting inference steps is used as the default policy, and that the default policy is executed for a fixed duration of 30 seconds.
quotes: Cyc’s existing mechanism for selecting inference steps (discussed above) is used as the default policy.
The default policy is executed for a fixed duration of time (set to 30 seconds).
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this setting of its own simulation algorithm.

assertions.value: The authors state that when a simulation reaches a terminal state it observes the number of answers R obtained, and N(s, a), N(s) and Q(s, a) are updated for every state-action pair on the simulation path, with Q(s, a) moved toward R by a step that shrinks with N(s, a).
quotes: the algorithm reaches a terminal state and observes the number of answers obtained from the simulation.
If R is the number of answers obtained from the simulation, then the following updates are made for any state action pair on the simulation path:
assertions.certainty_reason: The section defines the update rule used in training.
assertions.reader_inference: The reward is the number of answers found, not a binary success; equation (3) is an incremental-mean update, but the text layer scrambles its symbols.

assertions.value: The authors state that they used 2,698 features to represent an abstract state in the search space: 2,664 features for whether a certain argument of the focal literal is a sub-type of a given collection, 33 features for whether it is an instance of a given collection, and the depth of the sub-goal in the tree.
quotes: We used 2,698 features to represent an abstract
2,664 features were used to represent whether a certain argument of the focal literal
33 features were used to represent whether a certain argument of the focal literal is an instance of a given collection
the depth of the sub-goal in the tree
assertions.certainty_reason: The section states the state representation used in all experiments.
assertions.reader_inference: 2,664 plus 33 plus the depth feature equals 2,698, so the three groups are consistent.

assertions.value: The authors state that edges in the search space correspond to resolution steps that transform one node into another.
quotes: Edges in our search space correspond to resolution steps that transform one node into another.
assertions.certainty_reason: The section defines the search graph used.

assertions.value: The authors state that Q(s, a) is approximated by a partial tabular representation of visited state-action pairs, that this does not allow easy generalization between states, and that they therefore use a simple k-nearest neighbor algorithm, with Manhattan distance, to generalize from similar states.
quotes: we consider a simple k-nearest
In (4), NN(k, s) denotes the k-nearest neighbor of state s, where we use the Manhattan distance to compute the distance between two states.
assertions.certainty_reason: The section defines the learned heuristic module evaluated in the experiments.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper does not state the value of k used in the experiments.

assertions.value: The authors state that the resulting heuristic module uses the k-nearest neighbor algorithm on the output of the Monte Carlo tree search algorithm to evaluate the quality of inference steps, and that it is used to order inference steps.
quotes: This heuristic module uses the k-nearest neighbor algorithm on the output of the Monte Carlo tree search algorithm
we use this heuristic module to order inference steps and discuss its performance.
assertions.certainty_reason: The section defines the method whose performance is reported.

assertions.value: The authors state that the benchmark queries come from the real world and were created by knowledge engineers and programmers to test the performance of different applications and the inference engine, and that in most cases one answer was expected for a fully bound query.
quotes: These queries were created by the knowledge engineers and programmers to test the performance of different applications and the inference engine
In most cases, we were expected to find one answer for a fully bound query
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the source and form of its own test queries.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Cyc knowledge base has thousands of queries of various levels of difficulty, that they included problems from the group that require generation of a large search space and cannot be answered in several minutes, and that baseline results show many queries cannot be answered within 10 minutes.
quotes: The Cyc KB has thousands of queries of various levels of difficulty.
In this work, we have included problems from the latter group
results from the baseline experiments show that many queries cannot be answered within 10 minutes.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states how it selected its test problems.
assertions.reader_inference: The benchmark is biased toward hard queries by design, so the reported speedups apply to that selection, not to the average Cyc query.

assertions.value: The authors claim that the Cyc knowledge base is the largest and most expressive knowledge base that is amenable to deductive reasoning, so their algorithm has been tested on one of the most difficult reasoning problems.
quotes: the Cyc KB is the largest and most expressive knowledge base that is amenable to deductive reasoning
Therefore, our algorithm has been tested on one of the most difficult reasoning problems.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors, from the company that builds Cyc, describe their own product.

assertions.value: The authors state in a footnote that knowledge bases like ConceptNet might have more ground atomic formulas than the Cyc knowledge base but do not have axioms for deductive reasoning, and that researchers have shown Cyc-based problems are 1-3 orders of magnitude larger than other problems (citing Hoder and Voronkov).
quotes: KBs like ConceptNet might have more GAFs than the Cyc KB, but
they do not have axioms for deductive reasoning.
Researchers have shown that Cyc-based problems are 1-3 orders of magnitude larger than other problems
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that they divided the queries into four parts, used one part as the test set and the other three for training, and repeated this with each part to produce four experiments.
quotes: We divided the queries into four parts. One of the four parts was used as a test set, while the queries from the remaining three were used for training purposes
This process was repeated with each of the four parts to produce four experiments.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own evaluation protocol.
assertions.reader_inference: The query counts in Table 1 (266, 254, 261, 241) sum to 1022, and the Table 2 group counts also sum to 1022, so each query is a test query once. Splits are by query set, and the paper does not say whether related queries could fall in both train and test.

assertions.value: The authors define the speedup in experiment e as the time required by the inference engine to answer the queries under the baseline policy divided by the time it needs under the MCTS policy.
quotes: In the results, speedup in experiment e is defined as:
where Time( π, e) refers to the time required by the inference engine to answer queries in the experiment e when it uses the search policy π.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines the speedup measure its results use.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer does not say how time is aggregated or how unanswered queries, which hit the cutoff, are timed.

assertions.value: The authors report that the experimental data was collected on a 4-core 3.40 GHz Intel processor with 32 GB of RAM, and that the cutoff time for each query was restricted to 10 minutes.
quotes: The experimental data reported here was collected on a 4-core 3.40 GHz Intel processor with 32 GB of RAM.
restricted the cutoff time for each query to 10 minutes.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the hardware and cutoff of its own experiments.

assertions.value: The authors report for the first experiment in the first results table that the baseline answered 46% of 266 queries, and the best MCTS setting, with c set to 100 and 400,000 simulations, answered 92% of the queries with a speedup of 7.1 and a 100 percent improvement in the number of queries answered.
quotes: For example, in the first experiment we could answer 46% of 266 queries in the baseline experiment.
The best results from MCTS simulation was obtained when c was set to 100, and we allowed 400,000 simulations to learn the Q-values.
This led to a speedup of 7.1 and we could answer 92% of all queries.
assertions.certainty_reason: One empirical study on the authors' own query set; the best setting is chosen per experiment on the same test split.
assertions.reader_inference: Table 1 reports the best c and simulation count per experiment, with no separate validation split described, so the reported figures are best-of-sweep results on the test fold.

assertions.value: The authors report in the first results table for the second experiment that 254 queries were used, the baseline answered 66% of them, and the best MCTS setting, with c set to 10 and 500k simulations, answered 94% with a speedup of 5.4 and an improvement of 42 percent in queries answered.
quotes: Finally, the last column (labeled I(%)) shows the improvement in the number of queries answered w.r.t. to the baseline.
assertions.certainty_reason: One empirical study on the authors' own query set, best setting per experiment.
assertions.reader_inference: The columns are read from the Table 1 caption; the text layer prints the row cells in order.

assertions.value: The authors report in the first results table for the third experiment that 261 queries were used, the baseline answered 76% of them, and the best MCTS setting, with c set to 100 and 500k simulations, answered 94% with a speedup of 4.1 and an improvement of 24 percent in queries answered.
quotes: Finally, the last column (labeled I(%)) shows the improvement in the number of queries answered w.r.t. to the baseline.
assertions.certainty_reason: One empirical study on the authors' own query set, best setting per experiment.

assertions.value: The authors report in the first results table for the fourth experiment that 241 queries were used, the baseline answered 82% of them, and the best MCTS setting, with c set to 10 and 300k simulations, answered 94% with a speedup of 3.3 and an improvement of 14 percent in queries answered.
quotes: Finally, the last column (labeled I(%)) shows the improvement in the number of queries answered w.r.t. to the baseline.
assertions.certainty_reason: One empirical study on the authors' own query set, best setting per experiment.
assertions.reader_inference: Across the four experiments the speedup falls as the baseline answered share rises (7.1, 5.4, 4.1, 3.3 against 46, 66, 76, 82 percent), while MCTS answered 92 to 94 percent in all four.

assertions.value: The authors report that for a small number of simulations (about 100k), higher values of c (c = 1000) lead to the best performance, that performance then asymptotes soon, and that the best performance is obtained for small to medium values of c (c = 10 or 100).
quotes: For small number of simulations (~100k), higher values of c (i.e. c= 1000) lead to the best performance.
However, the performance asymptotes soon.
And the best performance is obtained for small to medium values of c (i.e. c = 10 or 100).
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical summary of one study; the figures that show it are images.

assertions.value: The authors state that the search policy learned from MCTS simulations leads to significant speedup compared to the baseline and to significant improvement in Q/A performance.
quotes: The search policy learned from MCTS simulations leads to significant speedup compared to the baseline.
MCTS-based learning has also led to significant improvement in the Q/A performance.
assertions.certainty_reason: A summary of results from one study on one knowledge base; no significance test is reported in the text.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper uses the word significant without a statistical test, and runs each configuration once per fold as far as the text says.

assertions.value: The authors report in the second results table that 597 queries needed 0 to 100 seconds in the baseline version, that the best speedup from MCTS simulations for those 597 queries was 1.23, and that there was no change in the number of answerable queries.
quotes: For example, there were 597 queries that needed between 0 and 100 seconds in the baseline version.
The best speedup obtained from MCTS simulations for these 597 queries was 1.23 and there was no change in the number of answerable queries.
assertions.certainty_reason: One empirical study, a sub-group result.

assertions.value: The authors report in Table 2, for six groups of queries ordered by increasing baseline time, speedups of 1.23, 3.33, 13.79, 11.79, 18.2 and 6.44, and percent improvements in the number of queries answered of 0, -2, 0, 0, 0 and 14600.
quotes: We also divided the query by the “degree of difficulty” as measured by the time required to answer them by the baseline version of the inference engine.
assertions.certainty_reason: One empirical study; the table cells are printed as columns in the text layer.
assertions.reader_inference: Read in order, the groups are 0-100, 101-200, 201-300, 301-400, 401-500 and over 500 seconds with 597, 50, 38, 9, 1 and 327 queries. The gain in answered queries sits almost entirely in the over-500-second group (14600 percent); the second group answered 2 percent fewer queries, the one reported loss. Speedup is lowest on the fastest queries (1.23).

assertions.value: The authors state that experimental results show the approach helps significantly reduce inference time and, by guiding search toward more promising parts of the tree, improves question-answering performance in time-constrained cognitive systems.
quotes: this approach helps in significantly reducing inference time
this approach improves the question-answering (Q/A) performance in time-constrained cognitive systems
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' summary of their own results.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that they proposed a sample-based search paradigm for learning search control knowledge, learning from simulated episodes sampled from the model, and that results for hundreds of queries from a very large and expressive knowledge base show a significant reduction in inference time and a notable improvement in Q/A performance.
quotes: we have proposed a sample-based search paradigm for learning search control knowledge
Results for hundreds of queries from a very large and expressive KB show that this approach can lead to a significant reduction in inference time.
It can also lead to notable improvement in Q/A performance.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' conclusion from one study on one knowledge base.

assertions.value: The authors state as future work that they want to test the methods on a larger set of queries to ensure their generality, to experiment with other schemes of feature selection because feature selection plays an important role in the performance of learning algorithms, and to design techniques to make Monte Carlo searches more efficient by including more domain knowledge in the simulation algorithm.
quotes: we want to test these methods on a larger set of queries to ensure their generality
since feature selection plays an important role in the performance of learning algorithms, we will experiment with other schemes of feature selection
we will design techniques to make Monte Carlo searches more efficient by including more domain knowledge in the simulation algorithm
assertions.certainty_reason: The Conclusions section names these open items itself.
assertions.reader_inference: The first item implies the authors do not yet regard the result as general beyond their query set.
